## QAQC Statement
The Company adheres to CIM Best Practices Guidelines for exploration-related activities conducted on its property. Quality Assurance and Quality Control (QA/QC) procedures are overseen by a Qualified Person. All geochemical sample assay results from Argenta Silver have been independently monitored through a rigorous QA/QC protocol. This protocol includes the regular insertion of blind standard reference materials, blanks, and duplicates. The logging and sampling of the El Quevar drill core were completed at Argenta’s core handling facilities in Salta, Argentina. Drill core was diamond-sawn on-site, and half drill-core samples were securely transported to Alex Stewart Laboratories’ (ASI) sample preparation facilities in Jujuy, and forwarded to their facility in Mendoza, Argentina for analysis. The other half-core is retained on site for reference. Soil samples were prepared by drying and sieving to minus 80 mesh. Rock chip and diamond drill core samples were dried and then underwent 2 stage crushing to 80% passing minus 10 mesh before collecting a 600 gram split that was pulverized to 90% passing -140 mesh. A 200 gram split is sent for analysis and the remaining 400g is archived. All samples were analyzed for gold using a fire assay on a 50-gram sample with an AAS finish, and for 39 elements by 4 acid, ICP-OES on a 0.2-gram sample. Soils were also analyzed for mercury using cold vapor AA on a 0.2-gram. Overlimit silver was determined by a 50-gram fire assay with a gravimetric finish and over limit lead, zinc and copper were determined by ICP_OES using a mixture of highly oxidizing acids on a 0.2-gram sample.

Soil samples were prepared by drying at <60°C and sieving to minus 80 mesh (code PREP-41). Rock chip samples were dried and then fine crushing of the sample to at least 70% passing less than 2 mm, sample splitting using a riffle splitter, and pulverizing a 250 g split to at least 85% passing 75 microns (code PREP- 31). Diamond drill core samples were dried and fine crushing of the sample to at least 70% passing less than 2 mm, sample splitting using a riffle splitter, and pulverizing a 1kg split to at least 85% passing 75 microns (code PREP-31B). All rock chip and diamond drill core samples were analyzed for gold using a fire assay on a 50-gram sample with an AAS finish, and for 35 elements by 4 acid, ICP-AES finish on a 0.75-gram sample plus mercury using cold vapor AA on a 0.2-gram (ME-ICP61m). Soils were also analyzed for gold fire assays and ICP-AES (Au-ICP21) and 48 multi-element four acid digestion with ICP-MS finish. Overlimit silver was determined by a 50-gram fire assay with a gravimetric finish and overlimit lead, zinc and copper were determined by OG62 using a mixture of highly oxidizing acids on a 0.4-gram sample.

el-quevar.name: El Quevar
el-quevar.intro: El Quevar is a 100%-owned, resource-stage silver project in the high Andes of Salta Province. Its main asset is the Yaxtché deposit, which contains 45.3 million indicated ounces of silver and 4.1 million inferred ounces. The wider property covers approximately 56,706 hectares and includes more than 20 exploration targets at different stages of advancement. Existing roads, a camp and nearby transport infrastructure support continued fieldwork.

sections.body: El Quevar lies in the Andean Central Volcanic Zone within the Quevar volcanic complex, where Miocene volcanic activity created the heat, structures and hydrothermal fluids associated with epithermal mineralization. Exploration has historically centred on Quevar South and Yaxtché, but current work extends across Quevar North and Azufre. Argenta acquired the full project through its purchase of Silex Argentina from Golden Minerals in 2024.

Yaxtché is a structurally controlled, silver-rich epithermal deposit hosted mainly by dacitic volcanic rocks, breccias and related intrusive or dome complexes. Mineralization occurs in zones of intense silicification and advanced argillic alteration associated with northwest–southeast and northeast–southwest faults. Silver is present in complex sulphide and sulphosalt minerals, with local gold and copper becoming more prominent toward targets such as Carmen.

brief.focus: The immediate technical question is whether drilling can convert recent step-outs into continuous extensions of Yaxtché while proving separate mineralized trends nearby. Work is concentrating on the northwest and southeast edges of the resource, the corridor toward Carmen and the Mani-Copan trend. Surface sampling, magnetic surveying and alteration mapping are also being used to rank the wider target pipeline.
brief.means: For investors, the deciding milestone is whether step-out drilling leads to a larger, updated mineral resource rather than a collection of isolated high-grade intercepts. Metallurgical work must also identify a repeatable processing route and acceptable recoveries. Those results would determine whether El Quevar can advance from resource expansion into formal economic studies.
brief.risks: El Quevar has no mineral reserve, economic study or demonstrated mine plan. Mineralization outside Yaxtché remains unevenly drilled, and high-grade intercepts do not establish the width, continuity or economics needed for resource conversion. Metallurgical behaviour varies across oxide, transition and sulphide material, while altitude, permitting, water management and long-term community support remain practical project risks.
brief.thesis: The project is being tested as more than a single isolated silver deposit. Argenta's working model is that Yaxtché and nearby targets formed within a broader hydrothermal system controlled by intersecting faults, volcanic centres and alteration zones. If that model is correct, high-grade silver may continue beyond the current resource and occur in additional structures across the property.

BRIEF_SECTIONS.v: Argenta explores the 100%-owned El Quevar silver project in Salta Province, Argentina. Its work centres on the existing Yaxtché mineral resource and a growing set of targets across the surrounding property.

Management is splitting the exploration program between expanding the known Yaxtché deposit and testing new mineralized zones elsewhere at El Quevar. Mapping, geochemistry, geophysics and drilling are being combined to move targets from early indications toward drill-tested prospects.

El Quevar already contains a defined high-grade silver resource, but the deposit occupies less than 1% of the 56,709-hectare property. Recent work has identified more than 20 targets and silver mineralization outside the current resource boundary, making the central question whether Yaxtché is one deposit within a broader mineralized district.

BRIEF_SECTIONS.v: The technical team is advancing resource-expansion drilling at Yaxtché while refining targets across Quevar South, Quevar North and Azufre. Metallurgical testing, magnetic surveying and environmental baseline work are running alongside the drill program.

The next stage would be supported by drilling that enlarges the Yaxtché resource or establishes continuity at nearby targets such as Mani-Copan. Metallurgical results must also show how the mineralization responds to potential processing methods before the project can move toward more advanced studies.
